L41:   * 【12†Further reading】
L42: Copilot CLI stores its configuration, session history, logs, and customizations in a single directory on your machine. By default, this directory is `~/.copilot` (that is, `$HOME/.copilot`).
L43: 
L44: This article describes the contents of this directory and how you can use them.
L45: ## 【4†Directory overview】
L46: 
L47: The `~/.copilot` directory contains the following top-level items.
L48: Path  | Type  | Description
L49: --- | --- | ---
L50: `agents/`  | Directory  | Personal custom agent definitions
L51: `config.json`  | File  | Automatically managed application state (authentication, installed plugins, and other internal data)
L52: `copilot-instructions.md`  | File  | Personal custom instructions (applied to all sessions)
L53: `extensions/`  | Directory  | Personal extensions loaded by the CLI
L54: `hooks/`  | Directory  | User-level hook scripts
L55: `ide/`  | Directory  | IDE integration state
L56: `installed-plugins/`  | Directory  | Installed plugin files
L57: `instructions/`  | Directory  | Additional personal `*.instructions.md` files
L58: `logs/`  | Directory  | Session log files
L59: `lsp-config.json`  | File  | User-level LSP server definitions
L60: `mcp-config.json`  | File  | User-level MCP server definitions
L61: `mcp-oauth-config/`  | Directory  | MCP OAuth token and registration fallback storage
L62: `mcp-secrets/`  | Directory  | Local fallback storage and index for MCP secret placeholders
L63: `permissions-config.json`  | File  | Saved tool and directory permissions per project
L64: `plugin-data/`  | Directory  | Persistent data for installed plugins
L65: `providers.json`  | File  | User-level bring-your-own-key (BYOK) provider and model registry
L66: `session-state/`  | Directory  | Session history and workspace data
L67: `command-history-state/`  | Directory  | Command history data
L68: `session-store.db`  | File  | SQLite database for cross-session data
L69: `settings.json`  | File  | Your personal configuration settings
L70: `skills/`  | Directory  | Personal custom skill definitions
L71: Note
L72: 
L73: Not all of these items appear immediately. Some are created on demand the first time you use a particular feature—for example, `installed-plugins/` appears only after you install your first plugin.
L74: ## 【5†User-editable files】
L75: 
L76: The following files are designed to be edited by you directly, or managed through CLI commands.
L77: ### 【13†`settings.json`】
L78: 
L79: This is the primary configuration file for Copilot CLI. Within a session, you can use the interactive `/settings` command to change specific values, or run `/settings KEY VALUE` to set a single value. See 【14†Changing settings with the /settings command】. Alternatively, you can edit the `settings.json` file directly in a text editor. The file supports JSON with comments (JSONC).
L80: By default, this file is located in the `~/.copilot` directory, which is the user-level configuration directory. It contains global user-level defaults for all repositories. You can change the location of this directory by setting the `COPILOT_HOME` environment variable to a different path.
L81: 
L82: Note
L83: User-editable settings are stored in `settings.json`. These settings were originally stored in `config.json`. Any user settings in `config.json` are ignored. That file is used to store internal state, such as installed plugins and trusted folders.
L84: If `settings.json` fails to read, parse, or validate, Copilot CLI ignores the invalid values and shows a startup warning on the timeline directing you to the Problems tab of the `/settings` command. Open that tab to see the specific error, then fix the reported issue to restore the affected settings.
L85: If `settings.json` contains a top-level key that isn't a recognized setting (for example, a typo), Copilot CLI lists it in the Problems tab of the `/settings` command instead of on the timeline or in stderr. The tab's label shows a count (for example, `Problems (2)`) when any configuration scope has an issue. `$schema` is tolerated and never reported.
L86: If `~/.copilot/settings.json` is a symlink—for example, to sync settings through a dotfiles repository—writes from the `/settings` command follow the symlink and update its target instead of replacing the symlink with a regular file.
L87: 
L88: For the full list of settings and how they interact with repository-level configuration, see 【9†Configuration file settings】 later in this article.
L89: 
L90: Tip
L91: 
L92: Run `copilot help config` in your terminal for a quick reference.
L93: Use `copilot config` from your shell, outside a session, to read or change settings non-interactively—the scripting counterpart to the `/settings` slash command. Add `--repo` or `--local` to target `.github/copilot/settings.json` or `.github/copilot/settings.local.json` instead of your user settings file; only 【15†repo-overridable keys】 can be written there. See 【16†GitHub Copilot CLI command reference】 for the full command reference.
L94: ### 【17†`copilot-instructions.md`】
L95: 
L96: Personal custom instructions that apply to all your sessions, regardless of which project you're working in. This file works the same way as a repository-level `copilot-instructions.md` but applies globally.
L97: 
L98: For more information, see 【18†Adding repository custom instructions for GitHub Copilot】.
L99: ### 【19†`instructions/`】
L100: 
L101: Store additional personal instruction files here as `*.instructions.md` files. These are loaded alongside `copilot-instructions.md` and apply to all your sessions. You can organize instructions by topic—for example, `~/.copilot/instructions/code-style.instructions.md`.
L102: ### 【20†`mcp-config.json`】
L103: 
L104: Defines MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers available at the user level. These servers are available in all your sessions, regardless of which project directory you're in. Project-level MCP configurations (in `.mcp.json` or `.github/mcp.json`) take precedence over user-level definitions when server names conflict.
L105: 
L106: For more information, see 【21†Adding MCP servers for GitHub Copilot CLI】.
L107: ### 【22†`lsp-config.json`】
L108: 
L109: Defines Language Server Protocol (LSP) servers available at the user level. These servers provide language intelligence (diagnostics, completions, etc.) to the agent. Manage this file using the `/lsp` slash command, or edit it directly.
L110: 
L111: For more information, see 【23†Adding LSP servers for GitHub Copilot CLI】.
L112: ### 【24†`providers.json`】
L113: 
L114: Defines a registry of bring-your-own-key (BYOK) providers and models, as a JSON object with `providers` and `models` keys. When this file declares any provider or model, it takes precedence over the legacy `COPILOT_PROVIDER_*` environment variables.
L115: 
L116: By default, this file is located at `~/.copilot/providers.json`. Override its location with the `COPILOT_PROVIDERS_CONFIG` environment variable.
L117: Models in this file are available alongside the models provided by your Copilot subscription. After editing the file manually, restart Copilot CLI to load your changes. For setup instructions, see 【25†Adding LLM models to GitHub Copilot CLI】.
L118: 
L119: Warning
L120: 
L121: API keys, bearer tokens, and header values in this file are stored as plain text. Do not commit the file to a repository or share it without removing credentials. Values such as `$MY_API_KEY` are literal strings, not references to environment variables.

L991: ### 【87†Managed permission rules】
L992: 
L993: Add `deny`, `ask`, and `allow` rule lists under the managed `permissions` key to enforce a permission policy for everyone. This works whether or not `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` is set.
L994: 
L995:     `{
L996:         "permissions": {
L997:             "deny": ["Shell(rm -rf *)", "Domain(*.evil.example)"],
L998:             "ask": ["Shell(git push *)"],
L999:             "allow": ["Read(**)"]
L1000:         }
L1001:     }
L1002:     `
L1003: Rule family  | Matches
L1004: --- | ---
L1005: `Bash(...)`, `Shell(...)`  | Shell commands. Use `<command> *` (for example, `git push *`) to match a command prefix; otherwise the rule matches exact text.
L1006: `PowerShell(...)`  | PowerShell commands, matched the same way as `Shell(...)`.
L1007: `Read(...)`  | File read/view paths. Supports glob patterns: `/` for the workspace root, `~/` for the home directory, and `./` for the current working directory.
L1008: `Edit(...)`, `Write(...)`  | File write/edit paths, matched the same way as `Read(...)`.
L1009: `Domain(...)`  | URL hostnames, matched like 【90†URL rules】.
L1010: Rules are combined across managed sources with a fixed precedence: deny always wins, then ask, then allow—matching a `deny` rule blocks the request even if an `allow` rule also matches. `deny` and `ask` are unioned across every managed source (server, MDM). `allow` requires every source that declares an `allow` list to admit the operation—an intersection, not a union.
L1011: When any of `deny`, `ask`, or `allow` is set, an operation that matches none of them defaults to `ask` rather than falling through silently.
L1012: `Edit(...)` and `Write(...)` rules apply to more than the built-in file tools. They also cover files written directly by a shell command. Copilot CLI recognizes a fixed set of these writes. It covers Bash output redirections (`>`, `>>`, `>|`, `&>`, `&>>`), PowerShell output redirections (`>`, `>>`, `*>`, `*>>`), and a small set of in-place `sed` edits (`sed -i` or `--in-place`, and the BSD forms `-i ''` and `-I ''`).
L1013: When Copilot CLI can work out the target file from the command, a matching `deny` rule blocks the write and a matching `ask` rule prompts you first. This applies even when a broad rule like `Shell(*)` would otherwise allow the command. Sometimes the target file cannot be worked out ahead of time, for example when the path comes from a variable. In that case these path rules do not apply, and the command is checked by the normal shell command rules instead.

L1015: 
L1016: Add a `limitTo` array alongside `deny`, `ask`, and `allow` under the managed `permissions` key to enforce a closed-world domain allowlist:
L1017: 
L1018:     `{
L1019:         "permissions": {
L1020:             "limitTo": ["github.com", "*.github.com"]
L1021:         }
L1022:     }
L1023:     `

The 【54†Decide what to enforce】 table lists the keys behind each control, and each entry in the 【56†settings reference】 says whether a managed source can set it. This file blocks two file reads, turns off bypass mode, and makes Claude Code ignore permission rules from user, project, and local files and from `--allowedTools`:

L126:       "permissions": {
L127:         "deny": [
L128:           "Read(./.env)",
L129:           "Read(./secrets/**)"
L130:         ],
L131:         "disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable"
L132:       },
L133:       "allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly": true
L134:     }
L135:     `
L136: 
L137: For a fuller example that shows the shape of more managed keys, including the login method, models, MCP servers, and marketplaces, see 【57†An organization’s managed settings】.
L138: 
L139: 2
L140: 
L141: Place the file on each machine
L142: Save the file as `managed-settings.json` in the system directory for the operating system, using whatever tooling already places files on your fleet:
L143: 
L144:   * macOS: `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json`
L145:   * Linux and WSL: `/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json`
L146:   * Windows: `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json`
L147: 
L148: 3
L149: 
L150: Confirm the policy applied
L151: On one machine, run `/status` inside Claude Code. The `Setting sources` line shows `Enterprise managed settings (file)`. Roll out to the rest of the fleet after that; 【45†Check that a policy is in force】 covers what to look at when the line is missing.
L152: ##
L153: 
L154: 【32†​】
L155: 
L156: Choose a delivery mechanism
L157: 
L158: The file in the steps above is one of four ways to get managed settings onto a machine. Every mechanism carries the same policy keys as a `settings.json` file, so the 【56†settings reference】 applies to all of them. A few keys are tied to particular sources, and each entry’s Scope line says which:
L159:   * Delivery controls: 【58†`policyHelper`】, 【59†`wslInheritsWindowsSettings`】, and 【60†`managedSourcesBehavior`】
L160:   * Gateway login keys: 【61†`forceLoginGatewayUrl`】, 【62†`gatewayInternalNetworks`】, and the `"gateway"` value of 【63†`forceLoginMethod`】
L161: A managed settings file, an MDM profile, or the claude.ai console applies one policy to everyone it reaches. To give one group of developers a different policy, deploy a different file or profile to that group; the claude.ai console 【64†can’t target a group yet】, while a self-hosted 【65†Claude apps gateway】 delivers managed settings per IdP group. When more than one mechanism delivers a policy to the same machine, Claude Code by default uses one and ignores the others.
L162: 【36†How Claude Code combines managed sources】 gives the order and the opt-in that applies every source. The MDM and file rows are together called endpoint-managed settings, because the policy is stored on the developer’s device, as opposed to the server-managed row, where Claude Code fetches it. Pick a mechanism by how you already manage devices, using the table below.
L163: Mechanism  | How you deliver it  | When Claude Code reads it  | Use it when
L164: --- | --- | --- | ---
L165: 【9†Server-managed settings】  | In the claude.ai admin console, or on a self-hosted 【65†Claude apps gateway】  | Fetched at startup and polled hourly; see 【33†changes that need approval】  | You want one place to change policy for a claude.ai organization without touching each machine
L191: ###
L192: 
L193: 【34†​】
L194: 
L195: Where each mechanism stores the policy
L196: 
L197: The keys are the same everywhere, but each mechanism stores them in a different place and shape:
L198:   * Server-managed: Anthropic’s servers, or your gateway, hold the policy. Claude Code keeps a local cache that it applies at startup and 【85†replaces on each successful fetch】.
L199:   * macOS configuration profile: the `com.anthropic.claudecode` managed preferences domain. Use the same top-level keys as `managed-settings.json`, with nested settings as dictionaries and lists as plist arrays.
L200:   * Windows HKLM registry: the JSON as a `REG_SZ` or `REG_EXPAND_SZ` value named `Settings` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode`.
L201:   * File-based: `managed-settings.json`, an optional `managed-settings.d/` directory, and `managed-mcp.json` in the system directory: `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/` on macOS, `/etc/claude-code/` on Linux and WSL, and `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\` on Windows. Claude Code doesn’t read the legacy Windows path `C:\ProgramData\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json`. You can deploy any of these files as a symbolic link, and Claude Code reads the file the link leads to.
L202: The policy still applies when the link leads outside the system directory or Claude Code can’t confirm that it stays inside. A warning naming the file then appears in `/status` and `claude doctor`. To clear the warning, point the link at a target inside the system directory.
L203:   * Windows HKCU registry: the same `Settings` value under `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode`.
L204: ###
L205: 
L206: 【35†​】
L207: 
L208: Split a file-based policy across teams
L209: If several teams own parts of one policy, put each part in its own file in `managed-settings.d/`, next to `managed-settings.json` in the same system directory, instead of editing one shared file. Claude Code merges `managed-settings.json` first, then every `*.json` file in the directory in alphabetical order. Name the files with numeric prefixes to control the order, such as `10-telemetry.json` and `20-security.json`. Claude Code ignores hidden files and files that don’t end in `.json`.

L240: 【37†​】
L241: 
L242: When an admin document counts as present
L243: 
L244: In the 【36†ranking of managed sources】, Claude Code never applies the user-writable HKCU registry beneath an admin document that is present. A document is present when:
L245:   * It sets any policy key to a value other than `null`, even a value Claude Code can’t read
L246:   * It is an HKLM value, managed settings file, or `managed-settings.d` directory that exists but can’t be read
L247: On WSL, `/etc/claude-code` is user-writable as well, and the 【59†`wslInheritsWindowsSettings`】 entry says when the Windows documents stand above it.
L248: ###
L249: 
L250: 【38†​】
L251: 
L252: Keys read from every admin source
L253: Under the default `"first-wins"` setting, Claude Code reads most keys only from the 【36†source it selected】, and ignores a value in a lower-ranked source even when the selected source leaves that key unset. A few keys work differently. Claude Code reads them from every admin source, so a lower-ranked MDM policy or managed settings file can still set them when the selected source doesn’t.
L254: Claude Code leaves the user-writable HKCU registry out of that scan; when HKCU is the only source and no host supplies parent settings, HKCU applies like any selected source. The cross-source keys include:
L255:   * `sandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnly` and `sandbox.filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly`: a `true` in any admin source turns the lock on. While a lock is on, Claude Code unions the allowlist it locks, `sandbox.network.allowedDomains` together with `WebFetch(domain:...)` allow rules, or `sandbox.filesystem.allowRead`, across every admin source. Without the lock, Claude Code treats the allowlist like any other key, so under `"first-wins"` an unselected admin source’s allowlist is ignored
L256:   * `allowAllClaudeAiMcps`
L257:   * `allowManagedMcpServersOnly`: a `true` in any admin source turns the MCP allowlist lock on. While the lock is on, the managed `allowedMcpServers` list comes from the highest-ranked admin source that sets one. A server-managed list replaces a lower source’s list rather than combining with it. If no admin source sets a list, every server that passes the denylist loads, unless 【42†parent settings】 supply a list.
L258: Without the lock, Claude Code reads `allowedMcpServers` from the managed source it applies, so under `"first-wins"` an unselected admin source’s list is ignored. Requires Claude Code v2.1.273 or later
L259:   * `deniedMcpServers` and 【93†`disableClaudeAiConnectors`】: an entry or a `true` in any admin source applies. Requires Claude Code v2.1.273 or later
L260:   * The sandbox binary paths `sandbox.bwrapPath` and `sandbox.socatPath`
L261:   * The sandbox `ripgrep` binary, 【94†`sandbox.ripgrep`】
L262:   * `sandbox.filesystem.disabled` and `sandbox.network.strictAllowlist`

L486: ##
L487: 
L488: 【51†​】
L489: 
L490: Turn telemetry off for your organization
L491: Claude Code sends Anthropic operational 【153†telemetry】 by default on sessions that use the Anthropic API, whether directly, through an LLM gateway, or through a custom `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`; 【154†Default behaviors by API provider】 says which providers send it. To turn it off for every developer without relying on each person’s shell, deliver `DISABLE_TELEMETRY` through the `env` block of your managed settings. This example sets `DISABLE_TELEMETRY` for everyone the policy reaches:
L492: 
L493:     `{
L494:       "env": {
L495:         "DISABLE_TELEMETRY": "1"
L496:       }
L497:     }
L498:     `
L499: Claude Code applies a value of `1` without showing the user the 【155†approval dialog】. If you turn telemetry off, Claude Code stops sending the usage data that feeds your organization’s 【24†analytics dashboard】 for the developers the policy reaches. The variable also turns off 【156†feature-flag fetching】 for those developers. For Remote Control, see the 【157†Remote Control requirements】.
L500: 【33†Where and when a policy applies】 says which delivery mechanism reaches each surface, and 【89†Platform availability】 says which sessions skip the server-managed settings fetch. If your organization uses customer-managed encryption keys and routes Claude Code through a gateway, 【158†Configure proxies and gateways】 says why those sessions need this variable.

L419: --- | ---
L420: `allowedMcpServers`  | Enforced as an empty allowlist until the value is fixed, so no MCP servers that users add are admitted. Servers your organization delivers through 【69†`managedMcpServers`】 still load, and `managed-mcp.json` servers load per 【118†Servers that skip the allowlist check】. An individual invalid entry is stripped and the valid subset is enforced.

L431: `deniedMcpServers`  | An individual invalid entry is stripped and the valid subset is enforced. A wholly invalid value is dropped with a warning, since denying every server would block servers the policy never named.
L432: 【125†`deniedModels`】  | A non-string entry is stripped and the rest of the list is enforced. A wholly invalid value is dropped with a warning and blocks no models until it is fixed.
L433: `blockedMarketplaces`  | An individual invalid entry is stripped and the valid subset is enforced. An entry that parses but can never match, such as a `hostPattern` regex that doesn’t compile, is kept with a warning. It blocks nothing until fixed, but 【78†marketplace restrictions】 stay active. A wholly invalid value is dropped with a warning, since blocking every marketplace would block sources the policy never named.
L434: `sandbox`  | When one value inside the block is invalid, Claude Code doesn’t drop the whole block. For what happens to each kind of invalid field, see 【49†Invalid values inside `sandbox`】.
L435: `sandbox.credentials`  | A recoverable invalid entry is degraded to `mode: "deny"` with a warning; an unrecoverable one is stripped; valid entries stay enforced. See 【126†invalid credential entries】.

The fallbacks for those two keys and for `allowedChannelPlugins` require Claude Code v2.1.267 or later; earlier versions drop the whole key when its value or any entry is invalid.

L442: 
L443: 【49†​】
L444: 
L445: Invalid values inside `sandbox`
L446: When one value in your managed `sandbox` block is invalid, Claude Code doesn’t drop the whole block, because it validates each field on its own. This per-field handling requires Claude Code v2.1.283 or later. On versions before v2.1.283, Claude Code drops every `sandbox` field except 【126†`credentials`】 when a value outside `credentials` is invalid. The warning you get for an invalid field names the field and tells you what happens to it. What happens depends on what the field controls:
L447:   * If you set a Boolean key to a quoted `"true"` or `"false"`, the value counts as that Boolean. Instead of a warning, `/status` shows a notice asking you to remove the quotes.
L448:   * If `failIfUnavailable` is invalid, Claude Code drops the value rather than treating it as `true`, so an unreadable value never stops sessions from starting across your fleet.
L449:   * Claude Code treats every other invalid Boolean as the value that keeps the sandbox strictest until you fix it. A key that turns the sandbox or one of its restrictions on, such as `enabled` or `network.allowManagedDomainsOnly`, counts as `true`. A key that loosens it, such as `allowUnsandboxedCommands`, counts as `false`.
L450:   * In a list outside `credentials`, such as `excludedCommands` or `network.allowedDomains`, Claude Code drops an invalid entry and keeps the rest of the list. A list that isn’t an array, or that has no valid entry, doesn’t apply at all.
L451:   * While `network.deniedDomains` or any entry in it is invalid, Claude Code also withholds `network.allowedDomains`, so the managed allowlist grants nothing until you fix the deny list.
L452:   * While `filesystem.denyRead`, `filesystem.denyWrite`, or any entry in either is invalid, Claude Code also withholds both `filesystem.allowRead` and `filesystem.allowWrite` until you fix the deny list.

L457: Keys only a managed source can set
L458: Claude Code reads the following keys only from a managed source; placing them in user or project settings files has no effect. Most of them are locks: the value a lock governs, such as permission rules or `sandbox.network.allowedDomains`, is an ordinary key that any level can set, and the lock tells Claude Code to honor only the managed value. The table covers the permission, plugin, and delivery controls.
L459: For any key not listed here, the Scope column of the 【127†settings reference】 index says whether it’s managed-only.
L460: Setting  | Description
L461: --- | ---
L462: 【128†`allowAllClaudeAiMcps`】  | Load the claude.ai connectors Claude Code fetches itself alongside a deployed `managed-mcp.json` instead of suppressing them
L463: 【129†`allowedChannelPlugins`】  | Allowlist of channel plugins that may push messages. Replaces the default Anthropic allowlist when set. Requires `channelsEnabled: true`. See 【130†Restrict which channel plugins can run】
L464: 【131†`allowManagedHooksOnly`】  | When `true`, restricts which hooks run; see 【132†what runs under `allowManagedHooksOnly`】 for the full effect list
L465: 【133†`allowManagedMcpServersOnly`】  | When `true`, only `allowedMcpServers` from managed settings are respected. `deniedMcpServers` still merges from all sources. See 【38†Keys read from every admin source】 for which managed sources can set it, and 【10†Managed MCP configuration】
L466: 【108†`allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`】  | Makes managed settings the only settings source of permission rules. The entry lists every source it ignores
L467: 【77†`blockedMarketplaces`】  | Blocklist of marketplace sources. Blocked sources are checked before downloading, so they never touch the filesystem. See 【78†managed marketplace restrictions】
L468: 【134†`channelsEnabled`】  | Allow 【135†channels】 for the organization. See 【136†enterprise controls】 for the default on each plan
L469: 【137†`disableCommandPluginSources`】  | When `true`, blocks 【138†`command` plugin sources】 entirely, so the marketplace-declared command never runs. Requires Claude Code v2.1.229 or later, and the `headersHelper` block requires v2.1.238 or later

comps_:

let
  # Remove components which are already installed by default
  filterPreInstalled =
    let
      preInstalledComponents = with components; [
        bq
        bq-nix
        core
        core-nix
        gcloud-deps
        gcloud
        gsutil
        gsutil-nix
      ];
    in
    builtins.filter (drv: !(builtins.elem drv preInstalledComponents));

  # Recursively build a list of components with their dependencies
  # TODO this could be made faster, it checks the dependencies too many times
  findDepsRecursive = lib.converge (
    drvs: lib.unique (drvs ++ (builtins.concatMap (drv: drv.dependencies) drvs))
  );

  # Components to install by default
  defaultComponents = with components; [
    alpha
    beta
  ];

  comps = [
    google-cloud-sdk
  ]
  ++ filterPreInstalled (findDepsRecursive (defaultComponents ++ comps_));

  installCheck =
    let
      compNames = map lib.getName comps_;
    in
    ''
      $out/bin/gcloud components list --only-local-state --format 'value(id)' > component_list.txt
      for comp in ${toString compNames}; do
        snapshot_file="$out/google-cloud-sdk/.install/$comp.snapshot.json"

        if ! [ -f "$snapshot_file"  ]; then
          echo "Failed to install component '$comp'"
          exit 1
        fi

        if grep --quiet '"is_hidden":true' "$snapshot_file"; then
          continue
        fi

        if ! grep --quiet "^$comp$" component_list.txt; then
          echo "Failed to install component '$comp'"
          exit 1
        fi
      done
    '';
in
# The `gcloud` entrypoint script has some custom logic to determine the "real" cloud sdk
# root. In order to not trip up this logic and still have the symlink joined root we copy
# over this file. Since this file also has a Python wrapper, we need to copy that as well.
symlinkJoin {
  name = "google-cloud-sdk-${google-cloud-sdk.version}";
  inherit (google-cloud-sdk) meta;

  paths = [
    google-cloud-sdk
  ]
  ++ comps;

  # Prevent Python from writing bytecode to ensure build determinism
  PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE = "1";

  postBuild = ''
    sed -i ';' $out/google-cloud-sdk/bin/.gcloud-wrapped
    sed -i -e "s#${google-cloud-sdk}#$out#" "$out/google-cloud-sdk/bin/gcloud"
    ${installCheck}
  '';
}

# default dependency which is undesirable because this package is

#   2) intended only for GCE guests (and is useless elsewhere)

{

  stdenv,
  lib,
  fetchurl,
  makeWrapper,
  python314,

  callPackage,
  installShellFiles,

  # NumPy is an optional runtime dependency and only needed for IAP TCP forwarding

  with-numpy ? true,

L1157:     browser_use_external = false
L1158:     in_app_browser = false
L1159:     in_app_updates = false
L1182: #### Disable Appshots
L1183: 
L1184: Appshots let supported clients include application snapshots. To disable them for cloud-managed users, open Edit as TOML in Agent security and set the top-level `allow_appshots` field in Global `requirements.toml`. For device-managed deployments, use the applicable local requirements source:
L1185: 
L1186:     `allow_appshots = false`
L1187: Where Appshots are available, `allow_appshots = false` disables them. If you omit the key, requirements don’t constrain Appshots, and normal product availability checks apply. App-server clients that read effective requirements through `configRequirements/read` receive the same restriction as `allowAppshots`; an omitted or `null` `allowAppshots` value doesn’t disable Appshots.
L1188: #### Disable device remote control
L1189: 
L1190: To disable 【569†device remote control】 for cloud-managed users, use Edit as TOML in Agent security and set the top-level `allow_remote_control` field in Global `requirements.toml`. You can also set `allow_remote_control` in a supported local requirements source:
L1191: 
L1192:     `allow_remote_control = false`
L1193: Where device remote control is supported, `allow_remote_control = false` disables it. If you omit the key, requirements don’t constrain device remote control, and normal product availability checks apply. This requirement doesn’t disable SSH remote connections.
L1194: ## Set approvals and execution permissions
L1195: 
L1196: Use this section to set approval behavior, permission boundaries, and starting defaults. Begin with 【555†Policy guardrails】 and 【556†Defaults】. The later tasks explain TOML requirements for reviewer enforcement, custom permission profiles, filesystem restrictions, host overrides, and command rules.
L1197: ### Admin-enforced requirements (requirements.toml)
L1198: Requirements constrain security-sensitive settings (approval policy, approvals reviewer, automatic review policy, sandbox mode, permission profiles, web search mode, managed hooks, which MCP servers users can enable, and which plugin marketplace sources they can use). When resolving configuration (for example from `config.toml`, 【570†profile files】, or CLI config overrides), if a value conflicts with an enforced rule, the local client falls back to a compatible value and notifies the user.
L1199: If you configure an `mcp_servers` allowlist, the client enables an MCP server only when both its name and identity match an approved entry; otherwise, the client disables it.
L1200: Requirements can also constrain 【566†feature flags】 via the `[features]` table in `requirements.toml`. Note that features aren’t always security-sensitive, but enterprises can pin values if desired. Omitted keys remain unconstrained.
L1201: 
L1202: For Codex 0.138.0 or later, prefer 【409†permission profiles】 with `allowed_permission_profiles` and managed `default_permissions`. Use `allowed_sandbox_modes` only for legacy deployments that still configure `sandbox_mode`.
L1203: For the exact key list, see the 【561†`requirements.toml` section in Configuration Reference】.
L1204: ### Set approval, sandbox, and web search guardrails
L1205: 
L1206: Use Requirements > Policy guardrails to limit supported client choices. These controls constrain configuration; they don’t select the starting value. Set the starting value separately under Defaults.
L1207:   1. In Global, open Approval policies and select the allowed approval styles. For example, Ask when needed allows the agent to request approval for actions such as sandbox escalation. Never ask prevents approval requests; it doesn’t grant unrestricted execution.
L1208:   2. Open Sandbox modes to limit legacy sandbox choices. Read-only restricts writes, Workspace write permits writes within the workspace and configured writable roots, and Full access removes filesystem sandboxing. Use 【571†permission-profile requirements】 for deployments that use permission profiles instead of `sandbox_mode`.
L1209:   3. In Global, open Web search modes to limit web search. Choose Cached to permit cached search without live search, or Disabled to turn off web search. Web search restrictions are separate from command network rules.
L1210:   4. Review the allowed choices and corresponding defaults, then select Save changes.
L1225: ### Example requirements.toml
L1226: 
L1227: This example blocks `--ask-for-approval never` and `--sandbox danger-full-access` (including `--yolo`):
L1228: 
L1229:     `allowed_approval_policies = ["untrusted", "on-request"]
L1230:     allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"]`
L1231: 
L1232: Here, `untrusted` preserves the stricter approval behavior derived from `trust_level = "untrusted"`; it does not make `approval_policy = "untrusted"` a supported explicit setting.
L1239: ### Configure automatic review policy
L1240: 
L1241: To make automatic review the default, use Global > Defaults > Command execution > Approval reviewer. A default lets users choose another permitted reviewer. To require automatic review or supply your organization’s review instructions, use Edit as TOML and edit Global `requirements.toml` instead. These requirements are separate from the browser’s automatic-review controls.
L1258: ### Control available permission profiles
L1259: 
L1260: Use Defaults > Command execution > Default permissions to choose the built-in profile users start with. To enforce which profiles users can select or to define custom profiles, use Edit as TOML and configure `requirements.toml` for the applicable Global or supported execution environment scope. Choosing a default alone doesn’t restrict the available profiles.
L1330: ### Enforce deny-read requirements
L1331: 
L1332: Use Edit as TOML to add filesystem restrictions to the applicable Global or supported execution environment `requirements.toml`. These restrictions block reads of sensitive paths; a read-only default by itself doesn’t hide files.
L1356: ### Enforce command rules from requirements
L1357: 
L1358: Use Edit as TOML in Agent security to add command rules and MCP server restrictions to Global `requirements.toml`. Command rules specify approval or denial decisions for matching commands; MCP restrictions limit which server identities the client can enable. The Approval policies control doesn’t author either of these rule sets.
L1359: Admins can also enforce restrictive command rules from `requirements.toml` using a `[rules]` table. These rules merge with regular `.rules` files, and the most restrictive decision still wins.
L1467: #### Other network runtime limits
L1468: 
L1469: All field names below are under `experimental_network` in `requirements.toml`. The arrows show a Global value followed by an environment value within the same policy. These local-execution cases do not establish Orchestrator support for the same settings.
L1482: Use `[application.network]` in `requirements.toml` to restrict the desktop app’s network destinations. With `enabled = true`, external requests must use HTTPS or WSS and match an exact domain with an `"allow"` value in `[application.network.domains]`. Subdomains aren’t implicitly allowed. An empty domain map permits no external destinations. See the 【374†Configuration Reference】 for the supported keys.
L1484: ## Configure plugins and managed hooks
L1485: 
L1486: For these tasks, use Edit as TOML in Agent security or a supported local configuration source. Marketplace defaults, enforced plugin restrictions, and managed hooks have different purposes; choose the task that matches the policy you need.
L1487: ### Configure plugin marketplaces and defaults
L1488: 
L1489: Use Agent security > Edit as TOML to define local or Git marketplaces and plugin defaults in the Global `config.toml` document. You can also distribute these settings in system `config.toml`. They provide starting marketplace and plugin configuration, not enforced policy. To limit which sources members can use, configure 【580†marketplace source requirements】.
L1490: See 【374†Configuration Reference】 for configuration keys, 【572†Configuration precedence】 for overrides, and 【581†repo plugin settings】 for project-level configuration. 【477†Workspace GitHub import and sync】 is separate.
L1491: ### Control plugin availability
L1492: 
L1493: Use Edit as TOML in Agent security for enforced plugin feature settings in Global `requirements.toml`, or distribute them through local requirements for device-managed clients. Defaults > Apps and tools > Apps/connectors sets app-tool defaults; it isn’t the enforced `features.plugins` switch. For workspace plugin permissions, see 【476†Apps and connectors】.
L1494: To turn off plugins in supported local clients, set `features.plugins` to `false` in `requirements.toml`:
L1495: 
L1496:     `features.plugins = false`
L1497: 
L1498: This setting also applies when users sign in to Codex with an API key. See the 【561†`features.plugins` reference】 for the supported configuration.
L1499: ### Restrict plugin marketplace sources
L1500: 
L1501: Use Edit as TOML to configure marketplace source requirements in Global `requirements.toml`, or deliver them through local requirements. These rules limit which local or Git sources users can add and use. They are separate from the 【582†marketplace defaults】.
L1502: To restrict plugin marketplace sources, set `restrict_to_allowed_sources = true` and define one or more source rules:
L1503: 
L1504:     `[…1002 tokens truncated…     [features]
L1542:     hooks = true
L1543: 
L1544:     [hooks]
L1545:     managed_dir = "/enterprise/hooks"
L1546:     windows_managed_dir = 'C:\enterprise\hooks'
L1547: 
L1548:     [[hooks.PreToolUse]]
L1549:     matcher = "^Bash$"
L1550:     [[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]]
L1551:     type = "command"
L1552:     command = "python3 /enterprise/hooks/pre_tool_use_policy.py"
L1553:     command_windows = 'py -3 C:\enterprise\hooks\pre_tool_use_policy.py'
L1554:     timeout = 30
L1555:     statusMessage = "Checking managed Bash command"`
L1556: Notes:
L1557: 
L1558:   * The local runtime enforces the hook configuration from `requirements.toml`, but it doesn’t distribute the scripts in `managed_dir`.
L1559:   * Deliver those scripts with your MDM or device-management solution.
L1560:   * Managed hook commands should reference absolute script paths under the configured managed directory.
L1561:   * `allow_managed_hooks_only = true` skips hooks from user, project, session, and plugin sources, but still loads hooks from `requirements.toml` and other managed config layers.
L1562: ## Understand policy scope and precedence
L1563: 
L1564: Use this section to check where a policy applies, how requirements combine, how clients receive cloud-managed settings, and how to verify the result.
L1565: For Work with local access and dots, supported Global policy governs the shared cloud orchestrator when managed policy is enabled; applicable local execution requirements govern the connected computer. Work cloud containers retain existing Work Cloud policies, and supported device controls still apply to local execution. Codex keeps its existing configuration behavior. Managed configuration does not grant a workspace seat or feature access. Use 【452†Roles and workspace permissions】 for those controls.
L1566: ### Agent Security and Local computer access with Work Cloud
L1567: 
L1577: Environment overrides vary supported settings within a policy. Within a given policy, the order from highest to lowest is OS-specific environment override → all-OS environment override → Global. A higher-priority policy still wins over a lower-priority policy, even when the lower-priority policy is more specific. Some requirements have field-specific merge rules. Confirm which override editors and fields are available for your workspace.
L1578: When managed policy and remote hooks are enabled, Work Cloud with local access and dots use admin-managed remote MCP hooks on the cloud orchestrator. Configure `mcp_tool` handlers in Global `requirements.toml`. Work Cloud without local access and personal accounts do not use these enterprise hooks.
L1579: Command/shell, prompt, and agent handlers; hooks from local configuration, plugins, or local directories; environment-scoped hooks; and `SessionEnd` MCP hooks are not supported with cloud orchestration, even when tools execute locally. When both orchestration and execution are local, existing supported hooks continue to work in local-only Work and Codex threads. Admins can still configure supported managed hooks in Agent Security for those workflows.
L1580: Before relying on these hooks, test callback connectivity, required events, and failure behavior. An explicit supported denial can block an action, but a `PreToolUse` callback error, timeout, or malformed response can fail the hook without blocking the tool. MCP hooks do not provide a complete Compliance API audit trail. See the 【374†Configuration Reference】.
L1581: ### Locations and precedence
L1582: 
L1583: For local execution, requirements are applied from lower to higher priority as follows. This ordering also applies to local steps in Local computer access with Work Cloud:
L1584:   1. System `requirements.toml` (`/etc/codex/requirements.toml` on Unix systems, including Linux and macOS, or `%ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml` on Windows).
L1585:   2. Agent Security requirements delivered in the cloud config bundle.
L1586:   3. Legacy `managed_config.toml` fields that the local client reinterprets as requirements.
L1587:   4. macOS managed preferences (MDM) delivered through `com.openai.codex:requirements_toml_base64`.
L1588: Higher-precedence layers override ordinary scalar and list values from lower layers. Tables merge by key, while requirements such as rules, hooks, and filesystem restrictions have field-specific composition behavior. Use the 【561†`requirements.toml` reference】 for the current schema instead of assuming that every field merges the same way.
L1589: For backward compatibility, supported local clients reinterpret the legacy `approval_policy`, `approvals_reviewer`, and `sandbox_mode` fields as requirements. This conversion adds compatibility choices where necessary; use `requirements.toml` for explicit allowlists.
L1590: ### Precedence for Local computer access with Work Cloud
L1591: 
L1592: For Work with local access and dots, distinguish Global orchestrator policy from execution policy. Applicable local requirements govern the connected computer. Work cloud containers and dots cloud computers use their own execution configuration and requirements, rather than the managed environment bundle used by other executors.
L1593: For local execution, MDM and legacy managed-device requirements rank above Agent Security. The device’s system requirements file ranks below Agent Security. Within each policy, resolve OS-specific environment overrides before all-OS environment overrides, then Global. Policy priority wins over specificity across policies.
L1594: Control  | Local Work without sync and local Codex  | Local computer access with Work Cloud
L1595: --- | --- | ---
L1596: Enterprise requirements  | Follow the local requirements order above.  | Apply to local executors. Work cloud containers retain existing Work Cloud policies.
L1597: Device execution restrictions  | Enforced by supported local controls.  | Follow the local requirements order above, including MDM and legacy requirements above Agent Security.
L1598: Environment overrides  | Use the configuration model for the relevant product.  | Within one policy: OS-specific environment override, then all-OS environment override, then Global. A lower-priority policy cannot win through specificity.
L1599: Requirements impose constraints, while configuration defaults supply starting values. For Work with local access and dots, supported Global policy applies through the shared cloud orchestrator when managed policy is enabled. Applicable local `requirements.toml` requirements govern execution on a connected computer. Work cloud containers and dots cloud computers use their own execution configuration and requirements, rather than the managed environment bundle used by other executor types.
L1600: Local execution restrictions do not automatically apply to these cloud computers. Review cloud capability permissions and test local and cloud execution separately.
L1601: Keep orchestrator controls, including approvals and web search, in Global. Use the dedicated Allowed approval policies and Allowed web search modes controls where available, and TOML for other supported fields. See the 【374†Configuration Reference】 for the field list and execution scope.
L1602: ### Cloud-managed requirements
L1603: 
L1604: When a user signs in with ChatGPT on a supported plan, supported local clients can receive admin-enforced requirements associated with the workspace. This is a delivery channel for `requirements.toml`-compatible policy. It doesn’t grant workspace access or replace workspace RBAC. Authentication requirements must be 【551†managed locally】.
L1605: Configure common requirements with the 【583†Agent security controls】. For a policy that allows only on-request approvals and read-only or workspace-write sandboxes, use Approval policies and Sandbox modes under Policy guardrails. To also prompt before a supported shell entry point runs, use Edit as TOML to add the `[rules]` table to Global `requirements.toml`.
L1606: The complete TOML equivalent is:
L1607: 
L1608:     `allowed_approval_policies = ["on-request"]
L1609:     allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"]
L1610: 
L1611:     [rules]
L1612:     prefix_rules = [
L1613:       { pattern = [{ any_of = ["bash", "sh", "zsh"] }], decision = "prompt", justification = "Require explicit approval for shell entry points" },
L1614:     ]`
L1615: Check that every managed client version supports the keys you select. Assign the policy to the intended users or groups and verify that it takes effect on their supported clients. Use the configuration reference for the current schema and the administration surface for current assignment behavior.
L1616: The service selects the enterprise-managed requirement layers that apply to the signed-in identity. The local client evaluates those layers with the other requirements sources described in 【563†Locations and precedence】. Use the current administration surface for workspace-side creation and assignment. Don’t rely on a copied group-matching algorithm; the administration service owns that behavior and can change it independently of the local requirements format.
L1617: For supported keys and examples, see 【584†Example requirements.toml】 and the 【561†`requirements.toml` reference】.
L1618: #### How local clients apply cloud-managed requirements
L1619: 
L1620: The local loading and cache behavior below describes supported local clients. It does not establish when a changed cloud policy takes effect in an already-running task using Local computer access with Work Cloud. Verify the effective policy before relying on a changed restriction.
L1621: When a user starts a supported local client and signs in with ChatGPT on a supported plan, the client first checks for a valid, identity-matched cache entry. If no valid entry is available, the client fetches the applicable bundle with retries and writes a signed cache entry on success. If the request fails or times out and no valid cache is available, the cloud config bundle load returns an error rather than silently starting without the cloud-managed requirements layer.
L1622: After cache resolution, the client composes the cloud requirements with the other requirements layers described above. A background refresh updates the cached bundle and makes it available to subsequent configuration loads. This doesn’t guarantee that an already-running task immediately uses a changed policy. Some desktop settings require an app restart; follow any restart prompt and verify the effective settings before relying on the change.
L1632: ### Manage authentication locally
L1633: 
L1634: Set `allowed_login_methods`, `allowed_chatgpt_workspaces`, `cli_auth_credentials_store`, and `chatgpt_base_url` in the local system `requirements.toml` or macOS MDM requirements. Codex ignores these four fields in cloud-managed requirements. Local authentication requirements apply before credentials load and before Codex retrieves cloud policy.
L1652: #### Precedence and layering
L1653: 
L1654: The local runtime assembles the effective configuration in this order (top overrides bottom):
L1655: 
L1656:   * Managed preferences (macOS MDM; highest precedence)
L1657:   * `managed_config.toml` (system/managed file)
L1658:   * `config.toml` (user’s base configuration)
L1659: 
L1660: CLI `--config key=value` overrides apply to the base, but managed layers override them. This means each run starts from the managed defaults even if you provide local flags.
L1661: Cloud `config.toml` uses 【572†normal configuration precedence】, not the legacy ordering above. Cloud `requirements.toml` uses 【563†requirements precedence】.
L1662: #### Locations
L1663: 
L1664:   * Linux/macOS (Unix): `/etc/codex/managed_config.toml`
L1665:   * Windows/non-Unix: `~/.codex/managed_config.toml`
L1666: 
L1667: If the file is missing, the local runtime skips the managed layer.
L1668: #### Example managed_config.toml
L1669: 
L1670:     `# Set conservative defaults
L1671:     approval_policy = "on-request"
L1672:     sandbox_mode    = "workspace-write"
L1673: 
L1674:     [sandbox_workspace_write]
L1675:     network_access = false             # keep network disabled unless explicitly allowed
L1676: 
L1677:     [otel]
L1678:     environment = "prod"
L1679:     exporter = "otlp-http"            # point at your collector
L1680:     log_user_prompt = false            # keep prompts redacted

L83: # Configure permissions
L84: 
L85: Control what Claude Code can access and do with fine-grained permission rules, modes, and managed policies.
L86: 
L87: Copy page Copy page
L88: 
L89: Claude Code supports fine-grained permissions so that you can specify exactly what the agent is allowed to do and what it can’t. You can check permission settings into version control to share them with every developer in your organization, and each developer can customize their own.
L90: ##
L91: 
L92: 【5†​】
L93: 
L94: Permission system
L95: 
L96: Claude Code uses a tiered permission system to balance power and safety. The table shows, for each tool type, whether Manual mode asks before the action runs. The other 【8†permission modes】 change which of these ask you; in auto mode a classifier reviews actions instead of you, and 【51†how the classifier evaluates actions】 lists which ones it sees.
L97: Tool type  | Example  | Approval required  | ”Yes, and don’t ask again” behavior
L98: --- | --- | --- | ---
L99: Read-only  | File reads, Grep  | No, within the 【39†working directory and additional directories】  | N/A
L100: Bash commands  | Shell execution  | Yes, except a built-in set of 【21†read-only commands】  | Permanently per repository and command
L101: File modification  | Edit/write files  | Yes  | Until session end
L102: Web fetch  | WebFetch  | Yes, except a built-in set of 【52†preapproved documentation domains】  | Permanently per repository and domain
L103: Web search  | WebSearch  | Yes  | Permanently per repository
L104: A permission prompt shows what Claude is about to do, followed by your options. This example is the prompt for a Bash command, from a session in Manual mode:
L105: 【53†Image: A Claude Code permission prompt titled Bash command. Under a tip about auto mode, it shows the description 'Run the test suite', the command npm test, and the line 'This command requires approval', then asks 'Do you want to proceed?' with four options: Yes; Yes, and don't ask again for: npm test *; Yes, and switch to auto mode; and No. A footer lists two keys: Esc to cancel and Tab to amend.†mintcdn.com】【54†Image: A Claude Code permission prompt titled Bash command.
L106: Under a tip about auto mode, it shows the description 'Run the test suite', the command npm test, and the line 'This command requires approval', then asks 'Do you want to proceed?' with four options: Yes; Yes, and don't ask again for: npm test *; Yes, and switch to auto mode; and No. A footer lists two keys: Esc to cancel and Tab to amend.†mintcdn.com】
L107: The third option, Yes, and switch to auto mode, 【55†doesn’t appear on every prompt】. When you choose “Yes, and don’t ask again” and the approval saves permanently, such as for a Bash command or a WebFetch domain, Claude Code saves the rule to `.claude/settings.local.json` at the root of the git repository, resolved through 【56†worktrees】 to the main checkout. The rule applies to future sessions anywhere in that repository, including sessions started in subdirectories and in worktrees.
L108: A file-modification approval isn’t saved to the file: as the table shows, it lasts until the session ends. In some cases, such as outside a git repository or on Windows, Claude Code doesn’t use the repository root; 【57†Where Claude Code looks for each file】 lists those cases and where it saves the rule instead. Sometimes a permission prompt offers only a one-time approval, with no “don’t ask again” option and no option to allow the action for the rest of the session.
L109: Claude Code offers those options only when the prompt can show you everything they would allow, so a rule you save from a prompt covers only what its option named. When a prompt offers only the one-time approval, approve the action once, or add the rule yourself in 【7†`/permissions`】. To stop the prompts for a command that starts with an exec wrapper such as `watch`, or for a `find` command with an action such as `-delete`, see 【19†Exec wrappers and `find` actions】.
L110: ###
L111: 
L112: 【6†​】
L113: 
L114: Add a comment when you answer a permission prompt
L115: You can attach a note to Claude when you approve or deny a single action. On most permission prompts, including Bash, PowerShell, file, and MCP tool prompts, move to Yes or No and press `Tab` to open a comment field on that option. WebFetch and browser prompts don’t offer the field. The options that allow the action for the rest of the session or save a rule don’t take one either. With the field open, type the comment and then press one of these keys:
L116:   * `Enter`: submits your answer with the comment attached. If you leave the field empty, Claude Code submits the answer without a comment.
L117:   * `Tab`: closes the field without answering. Claude Code keeps the text you typed and still sends it if you answer with that option.
L118:   * `Shift+Tab`: on a file prompt, such as an Edit or Write prompt, closes the field the same as `Tab`. Before v2.1.235, pressing `Shift+Tab` inside the field instead selected the option that allows the action for the rest of the session, so Claude Code approved the action for the rest of the session and discarded the comment.
L119: Claude Code delivers the comment differently depending on how you answered:
L120:   * Yes: Claude Code runs the action, then sends your comment to Claude after the result.
L121:   * No: Claude Code sends your comment to Claude as the reason for the denial, and Claude continues working. If you select No without a comment on a prompt from the main conversation, Claude Code stops the turn.
L122: ##
L123: 
L124: 【7†​】
L125: 
L126: Manage permissions
L127: 
L128: You can view and manage Claude Code’s tool permissions with `/permissions`. The dialog lists all permission rules and the `settings.json` file each rule comes from. You can open the dialog while Claude is working: when you add or remove a rule, Claude Code applies the change starting with Claude’s next tool call in the same turn. Before v2.1.234, Claude Code queued the command until the turn finished.
L129:   * Allow rules let Claude Code use the specified tool without manual approval.
L130:   * Ask rules prompt for confirmation whenever Claude Code tries to use the specified tool.
L131:   * Deny rules prevent Claude Code from using the specified tool.
L132: Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow. The first match in that order determines the outcome, and rule specificity doesn’t change the order. A broad deny rule like `Bash(aws *)` blocks every matching call, including calls that also match a narrower allow rule like `Bash(aws s3 ls)`. An allow rule can’t carve an exception out of a deny rule. The same precedence applies between ask and allow: a matching ask rule prompts even when a more specific allow rule also matches the same call.
L133: Deny rules behave differently depending on whether they name a tool or scope a pattern within one. A bare tool name like `Bash` removes the tool from Claude’s context entirely, so Claude never sees it. If you add such a rule mid-session, Claude can’t call the tool from its next tool call on; 【58†Denying an entire tool】 covers what happens to a definition Claude has already seen. A scoped rule like `Bash(rm *)` leaves the tool available and blocks matching calls when Claude attempts them.
L134: Bare-name removal applies to every tool except 【59†`EndConversation`】: a deny rule can’t remove it while any other tool remains, and an ask rule never prompts for it.
L135: Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model. Instructions in your prompt or `CLAUDE.md` shape what Claude tries to do, but they don’t change what Claude Code allows. To grant or revoke access, use `/permissions`, the rules described here, a 【60†permission mode】, or a 【36†PreToolUse hook】.
L136: 
L137: When 【61†auto mode】 is available to your session, the dialog also includes the 【62†auto mode classifier rules】. Select the Auto mode tab to view them.
L138: ##
L139: 
L140: 【8†​】
L141: 
L142: Permission modes
L143: 
L144: Claude Code supports several permission modes that control how it approves tool calls. See 【60†Permission modes】 for when to use each one. To change the mode sessions start in, set `defaultMode` in your 【63†settings files】. 【64†Which mode a session starts in】 covers the built-in default for each plan and what the VS Code extension reads.
L145: Mode  | Description
L146: --- | ---
L147: `default`  | Prompts for permission on first use of each tool. Labeled Manual in the CLI, the VS Code and JetBrains extensions, and the desktop app, and Claude Code accepts `manual` as an alias
L148: `acceptEdits`  | Automatically accepts file edits and common filesystem commands such as `mkdir`, `touch`, `mv`, and `cp` for paths in the working directory or `additionalDirectories`
L149: `plan`  | Claude reads files and runs read-only shell commands to explore but doesn’t edit your source files; with 【61†auto mode】 available, classifier-approved commands also run. Labeled Plan in the CLI and the VS Code extension
L150: `auto`  | Runs without routine prompts; before actions such as shell commands and network requests run, a background 【61†classifier】 checks that they align with your request
L151: `dontAsk`  | Auto-denies every call that would otherwise prompt, though a 【65†mod】 you installed can still approve some of those calls. File reads in your working directories and other actions that need no approval still run, as do tools pre-approved via `/permissions` or `permissions.allow` rules.
L152: `AskUserQuestion`, MCP tools marked 【66†`requiresUserInteraction`】, 【30†reads from network paths】, and connector tools 【67†your organization set to `ask`】 in sessions where that setting reaches Claude Code are denied even if you’ve allowed them
L153: `bypassPermissions`  | Skips permission prompts, except for the 【68†actions no mode auto-approves】
L154: In `bypassPermissions` mode, Claude Code skips permission prompts, including for writes to 【69†protected paths】 such as `.git` and `.claude`. The 【70†cross-session messaging safeguards】 still apply. Only use this mode in isolated environments like containers or VMs where Claude Code can’t cause damage.
L155: To prevent `bypassPermissions` or `auto` mode from being used, set `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` or `permissions.disableAutoMode` to `"disable"` in any 【63†settings file】. These are most useful in 【44†managed settings】 where they can’t be overridden.
L156: ##
L157: 
L158: 【9†​】
L159: 
L160: Permission rule syntax
L161: 
L162: Permission rules follow the format `Tool` or `Tool(specifier)`. Parentheses inside the specifier are literal, so a command or path that contains them needs no escaping.
L163: ###
L164: 
L165: 【10†​】
L166: 
L167: Match all uses of a tool
L168: 
L169: To match all uses of a tool, use only the tool name without parentheses:
L170: 
L171: Rule  | Effect
L172: --- | ---
L173: `Bash`  | Matches all Bash commands
L174: `WebFetch`  | Matches all web fetch requests
L175: `Read`  | Matches all file reads
L176: `Bash(*)` is equivalent to `Bash` and matches all Bash commands. As a deny rule, both forms remove the tool from Claude’s context. The label shown for a tool in the transcript and permission dialog can differ from its canonical name. For example, the tool labeled `Stop Task` in the transcript has the canonical name `TaskStop`. Permission rules and 【71†hook matchers】 don’t match the label, so a rule written as `Stop Task` doesn’t match. For deny and ask rules, a 【72†startup warning】 says so.
L177: Use the canonical names listed in the 【73†tools reference】.
L178: ###
L179: 
L180: 【11†​】
L181: 
L182: Use specifiers for fine-grained control
L183: 
L184: Add a specifier in parentheses to match specific tool uses:
L185: 
L186: Rule  | Effect
L187: --- | ---
L188: `Bash(npm run build)`  | Matches the exact command `npm run build`
L189: `Read(./.env)`  | Matches reading the `.env` file in the current directory
L190: `WebFetch(domain:example.com)`  | Matches fetch requests to example.com
L191: ###
L192: 
L193: 【12†​】
L194: 
L195: Match by input parameter
L196: Deny and ask rules can match a top-level input parameter on any built-in tool with `Tool(param:value)`. To match a parameter on an MCP tool, pass a deny rule with 【74†`--disallowedTools`】. When Claude Code loads a settings file, it skips any `mcp__` rule that has parentheses. Claude Code lists the skipped rule in the invalid-settings dialog when an interactive session starts, and in 【75†`claude doctor`】 output. A parameter rule matches when Claude calls the tool with that parameter set to that exact value.
L197: An allow rule for one parameter value wouldn’t establish that the call is safe overall, so allow rules continue to use each tool’s own specifier syntax. This works for any scalar parameter the tool accepts:
L198: Rule  | Matches
"}

  copilotArgs = lib.concatMapStringsSep " "
    (command: lib.escapeShellArg "--deny-tool=shell(${command}:*)" + " "
      + lib.escapeShellArg "--deny-tool=shell(${command})")
    commands;

  # Most restrictive wins, even against a repository's matching allow rule.
  codexRules = lib.concatMapStringsSep "\n" (pattern: ''
    prefix_rule(
        pattern = ${builtins.toJSON pattern},
        decision = "forbidden",
        justification = "Google Cloud PAM commands are disabled on this machine.",
    )
  '') tokens;

  codexRequirements = lib.concatMapStringsSep "\n" (pattern: ''
    [[rules.prefix_rules]]
    pattern = [${lib.concatMapStringsSep ", " (token: "{ token = ${builtins.toJSON token} }") pattern}]
    decision = "forbidden"
    justification = "Google Cloud PAM commands are disabled on this machine."
  '') tokens;
}
  '';

  doInstallCheck = true;

    # Avoid trying to write logs to homeless-shelter
    export HOME=$(mktemp -d)
    $out/bin/gcloud version --format json | jq '."Google Cloud SDK"' | grep "${version}"
    $out/bin/gcloud storage ls --help > /dev/null
    # Exercises generated clients that use Cloud SDK's vendored protobuf. This
    # catches regressions where external protobuf/upb is selected instead of the
    # vendored pure-Python protobuf implementation.
    $out/bin/gcloud kms asymmetric-sign --help > /dev/null
    PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=upb $out/bin/gcloud kms asymmetric-sign --help > /dev/null
    $out/bin/gsutil version | grep -w "$(cat platform/gsutil/VERSION)"
    # byte-code must exist at the path python looks up with the wrapper's CLOUDSDK_PYTHON_ARGS
    ${pythonEnv}/bin/python -S -B -c 'import importlib.util, os, sys; sys.exit(not os.path.exists(importlib.util.cache_from_source(sys.argv[1])))' \
      $out/google-cloud-sdk/lib/gcloud.py
  '';

  postFixup = ''

      echo "rewriting certificate bundle: $f"
      ln -sf ${cacert}/etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt "$f"

# .dotfiles

NixOS configuration for `thixos`, a WSL2-based development machine.

## Repository Structure

```
.dotfiles/
├── flake.nix              # Top-level flake: NixOS config + inputs
├── flake.lock
├── nixos/
│   └── configuration.nix  # System config (~700 lines, the core of everything)
├── config/
│   ├── zellij/            # Zellij config, layouts, plugin config
│   ├── starship.toml      # Shell prompt
│   └── windows-terminal.json # Terminal emulator (runs on Windows, copied via script)
├── bespoke/
│   └── zellij/
│       └── dim-unfocused/ # Custom Zellij build + shader plugin (has its own AGENTS.md)
├── templates/             # Nix flake templates
└── .zshrc, .gitconfig, etc.
```

## How It Builds

The top-level `flake.nix` produces a single NixOS configuration (`thixos`):

- **Inputs**: `nixpkgs` (unstable), `nixos-wsl`, `llm-agents` (Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex, Grok, Copilot), `dim-unfocused` (local path flake for custom Zellij)
- **Output**: `nixosConfigurations.thixos`

The `dim-unfocused` sub-flake (at `bespoke/zellij/dim-unfocused/`) has its own inputs including a Zellij fork. It produces a custom Zellij binary and a WASM plugin. See `bespoke/zellij/dim-unfocused/AGENTS.md` for deep details on the shader system.

### Deploying changes

```bash
# For NixOS
sudo nixos-rebuild switch --flake ~/src/github.com/tteggel/.dotfiles#thixos

# For Standalone / Ubuntu
home-manager switch --impure --flake ~/src/github.com/tteggel/.dotfiles#thom@nix
```

## configuration.nix and home.nix

This is the heart of the system. `nixos/configuration.nix` sets up OS-level features, while `home/home.nix` defines the user environment:

### Custom shell scripts (in home.nix)

The configuration embeds several substantial shell applications as `writeShellApplication` derivations:

- **`session-picker`** — Zellij session manager. Lists existing sessions, creates new ones, clones GitHub repos. Launched on shell login.
- **`command-palette`** — Context-aware fzf command launcher with ~25 commands. Invoked via Zellij keybinding.
- **`code-session`** — Open the code layout in Zellij (agents launch fresh; resume via each agent's own native picker). Repos under `~/src/github.com/bookcreator/` get `code-copilot.kdl` instead, with two Copilot CLIs (Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, xhigh, autopilot) in place of Claude and Codex; `session-picker` makes the same choice for new sessions.
- **`gcloud-switch`**, **`gcloud-reauth`** — GCP project/cluster switching.
- **`zed`** — Interop wrapper to launch Windows Zed editor from WSL.
- **`open-browser`** — Opens URLs in Windows Chrome from WSL.

### Shell environment (zsh)

- Starship prompt
- Auto-attaches to Zellij on login
- Zoxide + fzf for directory navigation
- Dynamic pane titles (`repo:branch` format via precmd/preexec hooks)
- Environment: `ZELLIJ_CONFIG_DIR`, `BROWSER`, `EDITOR` / `VISUAL` (hx/Helix), `MANPAGER` (bat), `NODE_OPTIONS` (preloads `config/node/ipv4-listen.js` so host-less Node `listen` binds IPv4, see the README's WSL networking section)

### System packages

Dev tools (zellij, git, gh, ripgrep, fd, bat, eza, delta, lazygit, helix, difftastic), cloud tools (gcloud, kubectl), LLM agents (claude-code, antigravity/agy, codex, grok, copilot).

### Config file management

Files from `config/` are symlinked into `~/.config/` via Home Manager's `xdg.configFile`. The Windows Terminal config is copied to the Windows filesystem via NixOS activation scripts (NixOS only).

## Working with this repo

- **Zellij is custom-built** from a fork with pane shader support. Don't update the `dim-unfocused` flake input without checking the fork is in sync. See `bespoke/zellij/dim-unfocused/AGENTS.md`.
- **Zellij rebuild takes ~20 minutes** (Rust). Avoid changes to the fork unless necessary. The plugin and shader WASM rebuild in seconds.
- **The `config/zellij/config.kdl`** loads the dim-unfocused plugin. If the plugin WASM path changes, update it there.
- **Shell scripts in `configuration.nix`** are the most frequently edited part. They rebuild instantly with `nswitch`.
- **Flake lock updates**: The top-level lock pins transitive inputs from sub-flakes. After updating `bespoke/zellij/dim-unfocused/flake.lock`, also run `nix flake update` at the top level to propagate.
